Some identifiers in the current bug report may be anonymized with placeholders (e.g., C#.M#). Always confirm actual identifiers by inspecting the source code using get_code_snippet.

You will be given 9 opportunities to interact with functions to gather information for the debugging. An example diagnosis would look like follows.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: The corresponding issue report describes that tooltip text in the UI is displayed with HTML entities such as " instead of the intended characters. This strongly suggests a missing escaping or decoding step in tooltip generation. Inspecting the implementation of StandardToolTipTagFragmentGenerator.generateToolTipFragment reveals that it directly returns the toolTipText without applying any escaping. Recent issue reports mention similar encoding or escaping problems in related UI components, reinforcing the suspicion that this method lacks proper handling. The behavior observed in the code matches the issue report's symptoms, indicating that missing escaping in this method is the likely root cause.

After providing this diagnosis, you will be prompted to suggest which methods would be the best locations to be fixed. The answers should be in the form of `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` without commentary (one per line), as your answer will be automatically processed before finally being presented to the user.

messages.content:
Diagnosis:
The test failure is related to the method `DurationFormatUtils.formatPeriod(long, long, String)`. This method delegates the operation to an overloaded version with more parameters, which then calculates the difference between two timestamps in terms of years, months, days, hours, minutes, seconds, and milliseconds.

The period is calculated by breaking down the difference between endMillis and startMillis into Calendar fields. This breakdown involves subtracting corresponding fields from the "start" and "end" Calendar objects (representing the start time and end time in the specified timezone). The initial differences are further adjusted by rolling negative differences from smaller to larger units (e.g., milliseconds to seconds, seconds to minutes, etc.).

Of particular note is the handling of days. When adjusting negative values of days, the code adds 31 days regardless of the actual month's length (`days += 31;`). This hardcoded 31 is followed by a comment noting this as a tricky issue (lines 307-311), acknowledging that day counting can be contextual and that there are complexities related to months with different lengths (not all months have 31 days).

The `reduceAndCorrect()` method is used to further refine differences by adjusting "end" Calendar fields and correcting the differences if the "end" field values fall behind the "start" ones.

The test case sets the start date to December 31, 2005, and the end date to October 6, 2006. The expected difference in months is "09". However, as the hardcoded days addition uses 31 instead of the actual number of days in December or January and given that December 31 is at the end of a month with 31 days, the calculation might incorrectly shift months/days and cause incorrect results. The fact that it is "only when Date is set to Dec 31, 2005" aligns with the root cause being the treatment of the day difference with a fixed 31 days, leading to under or over-counting resulting in the wrong number of months being calculated.

Thus, the bug is caused by the faulty assumption about the number of days when correcting negative days difference — specifically the hardcoded addition of 31 days ignoring the actual varying lengths of months, leading to an incorrect calculation of the period between the dates starting on Dec 31, 2005. The code needs a more nuanced approach that accounts for the actual number of days in the months involved in the calculation.

Next, I can check if there is code dealing with how many days to add or if other parts of adjustment can be improved.

org.apache.commons.lang.time.DurationFormatUtils.reduceAndCorrect(java.util.Calendar,java.util.Calendar,int,int)
